idiom_name: one small always-invoked decision component with a replaceable policy source behind an explicit trust boundary
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: isolate one component whose only job is to decide and enforce access, keep its state private and its interface enumerated, and place it where the code it polices cannot reach it - a kernel or LSM hook, a hypervisor, a privilege-separated process, a container or an OS sandbox. All rules live in a replaceable policy source that the monitor reads but never owns, so a policy change never touches the verified core; the identity the monitor decides about comes from a source the caller cannot forge, and the monitor denies by default - missing identity, unreachable policy and internal errors all refuse. Perform the access in the same operation as the decision so that no check-then-use window remains, and hand out only mediated operations: a raw reference (descriptor, pointer, connection, path, mutable copy) that escapes after a granted decision is an unmediated route to the resource. Keep the monitor small enough that every mediated operation can be enumerated, and keep that enumeration next to the tests, so that each addition to the trusted core is a visible change to the verification argument.
code_sketch:
decision = monitor.decide(subject, action, object)      # one small core
# requirements the structure has to satisfy:
#   always invoked  -> the resource is reachable only through the monitor
#   tamperproof     -> the monitor sits outside the reach of the code it polices
#                      (kernel hook, privilege-separated process, sandbox, hypervisor)
#   verifiable      -> enumerated operations, own test suite, policy kept in a
#                      replaceable source outside the core
# fail closed: an unresolvable identity or policy is a denial, never a pass
if decision is allow:
    perform(object, action)            # check and use are one operation
pitfalls: Claiming tamper resistance in-process: the same address space, reflection, agents, loader hooks and monkey patching all reach a monitor that is not behind a real boundary.
Letting a raw reference escape after the decision, which reduces the monitor to a guard the next access never passes.
Growing the monitor into a policy engine: every rule that lives inside it subtracts from the verification argument the pattern exists to make.
Failing open on a missing identity, an unreachable policy or an internal error.
Shipping without the evidence: no enumeration of mediated operations, no isolated test suite, no tests that try to reach the resource around the monitor.

Wrong move: cache an allow decision while identity or policy can change -> revocation and ownership changes bypass complete mediation -> instead bind the decision to a subject/object version or revalidate at each access boundary.

Wrong move: let a privileged broker act on caller-supplied object IDs without preserving caller identity -> a confused deputy reaches objects the caller could not -> instead carry an unforgeable subject context and authorize the exact object/action in the monitor.

Wrong move: leave a raw syscall, shared-memory queue or alternate administrative API beside the monitored entry point -> traffic around that hook is never mediated -> instead enumerate every resource entry point and move the boundary below them or remove the bypass.
